utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tadic. We will continue. We spoke about the first exchange at Zasavica and my final question is this: Given that in your interview to the OTP on page 71, you mentioned that you learned later on that Croats refused to release ten Serbs who had also been brought to Zasavica. When was it that you heard about that, that they were not able to cross over in that exchange, they were not allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first knowledge was gained on that very day when we saw that a fewer number of people came than was initially planned. However, we were not quite sure what was behind this. I learned of this later with the next exchange on the 4th of July, when the people who were returned on the first occasion came, and then they told us that they were at the exchange site but that due to some reasons, they were returned, and at the time they didn't know why they were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following that exchange, did you continue negotiations regarding the ensuing exchanges? Where did you go for negotiations and whom did you negotiate with?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours could we move into private session before the witness gives his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you continue negotiating and where were these negotiations conducted and what was the purpose of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 25th or 26th of May, we learned from the people who were exchanged then a lot of new facts that were important, and we wanted to continue with our negotiations in order to have some more activity of that nature. Mr. Mikic, a few days later, told me that another man would come who would talk to me, and that was this very gentleman that we have mentioned. We continued our negotiations concerning the upcoming exchange. At the time I did not know the gentleman, so it was a bit tense, the situation was a bit tense. There was a bit of mistrust there. However, we had no other option. We had to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were these talks conducted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The talks were still conducted through the communication centre so we had no direct contact except the contact through communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have heard Mr. Ninkovic and Mr. Maslic testify about the communication centre. Let us just point out for the Trial Chamber that this communication centre was linked throughout the region with several other centres and that was how it was before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ninkovic spoke about this and he is more informed than anyone else and he said that before the war, this communication centre was used to establish contact between various municipalities in our region. This region is called the Doboj region. I don't want to enumerate these municipalities it's already been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The official name of that centre was the centre for early warning and reporting is that what it was called?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what Mr. Ninkovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we will refer to as the communication centre because that is how it is generally known.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness be shown document PDB 141? That's how it is internally marked, 141/ter. That's the last document that was delivered in this particular set of documents. The witness will speak of this document. He knows quite a lot about it. Your Honours, you have the original document, as it was drafted, then there is a version in B/C/S and the translation into English. I saw several errors in the B/C/S version that were later reflected in the English version as well. And I would like now to go with the witness over five reports. I believe this document to be very important, not only for Mr. Tadic's Defence but also in order to clearly show what the situation was like in Samac. What you can see, Your Honours, is that up until the 17th of April, there are only certain hours given in certain reports, and after the first several pages, you will see that the dates are missing and then after the month of June, the reports were made -- the entries were made on a daily basis and in order to cover this quickly, Mr. Tadic, I will read this out to you and you can just confirm to me whether it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first part I would like to read out is on the English version, page 7, paragraph 4. And it begins with the 30th of June. The 30th of June, if you've found that entry, then I would start reading out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which document? We can't find the -- page 7, we can't find 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can't find it either, if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the French booth does not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic the French booth say they don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Neither does the English booth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English version at the end, page 7 is marked, page 7 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, we have a problem with the ELMO. We don't receive any picture here. So in the meantime maybe we could have assistance of the technical booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have a question because there are no number attached, do you mean this thick document, what is a handwritten first part and then it's -- there is a B/C/S version and an English version and it's the document dated on the 6th of December, 1992? Is that the document we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. In the original B/C/S version, which is handwritten, you will see that the 6 December of 1992 is written in a handwriting, in the upper corner, but the date mentioned is the 26th of November, and the witness will tell us about that. That is the document, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I may continue, Your Honour, on page 7 we can't find what you was -- you were pointing to. There is no paragraph 4. There is three dates, 6 of February, 7th of February and 10th of February and then no dates at all except for, yeah, they are 12th of February, 13th of February and 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please take a look at page 7 of the English version. Do you have an English version marked on page 7? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that page, or rather -- I'm sorry, page 4, page 4, paragraph 3, [In English] [Microphone not activated] 30 June. [Interpretation] On the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No, there is nothing such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could we have the usher's assistance, maybe the usher should show you the document we have. Mr. Lukic can look at it and see whether that's the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the transcript was done later on, the pages in your versions are differently marked. Let us leave aside this document and during the break, I will compare the pages and then we can analyse this document after the break. It will be easier for everybody to follow. In the meantime we can cover other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the initial translation and this is how I did my marking but during the break I will get everything ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we will come back to this document after the break. Tell us, please: What did you negotiate about with the opposite side? What was the procedure like and what did you do after the negotiations in order to carry out an exchange successfully?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we talked about the events which took place on the 25th of May so we talked about the first exchange, and jointly we concluded that as far as the technical matters were concerned, that exchange was not a great success. There were problems with crossing over at the exchange site. The river itself, the River Bosna, presented quite a problem. At the time the water level was quite high, and the terrain on the opposite side was quite muddy so the access was not an easy one. Another problem was that at the time we found ourselves right between two defence lines, if I can call them that way, behind our back were the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska, whereas behind the back of the people on the other side were the soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council. So a minor incident, not a deliberate one, could have put both sides in a very difficult situation. Therefore, we concluded that we shouldn't have any other activities at that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did somebody propose something? Did somebody give an initial proposal and where did you start meeting after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some time, given that the opposite side had already had talks with the 1st Krajina Corps, with which we had no contact whatsoever, there was part of the core that was stationed in Banja Luka at the time, in the Banja Luka area. So as a result of that, they already had some experience with that and they used to meet in a place called Dragalic, which is a gas station on the former highway between Belgrade and Zagreb, some 30 kilometres from Slavonski Brod in the direction of Zagreb. There was another site on the eastern part of that area, near a town called Sid, the place was called Lipovac. They suggested that we conduct the following exchange in Lipovac. At the time it was an UNPA zone. That's what it was called. It was under the control of the United Nations. I believe that there was a Russian battalion there in addition to other forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. We will now analyse these two issues but before we do that, it would be good to put a map before the witness. This was a map presented during the testimony of Dr. Donia showing UNPA zones. Perhaps the witness could now show us where Samac is and where these other two places, Sid and Lipovac are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the document's formal exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly but it was attached to the expert report of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we just have the number from the registry, please, assistance? If you can search so that we know exactly which map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly but it was attached to the expert report. I don't know if Dr. Donia specifically mentioned this. This is map number 13, showing Bosnia and Herzegovina and the UNPA protected zones. I have the OTP number here. Perhaps they would be able to help us, 03019614 is the number, since this is an OTP exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That can't help us at the moment to identify it. Am I right if Mr. Lukic intends to have it marked and present it as a fresh new exhibit? Or if that's the case, we don't need to know what the old number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It was attached to the report, I'm informed, which was Exhibit -- which is Exhibit P1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that Mr. Lukic intends to create now an entirely new exhibit because it's going to be marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's map 13 of Exhibit P1, I think. Yes, the correct information now Dr. Donia's report is P1, all the maps collectively are P2. So it's part of P2. So your intention is to have that clear map marked by the accused and then it will be exhibit -- it will be an exhibit for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, if you can just roughly mark with number 1, Samac, Dragalic with number 2, and Lipovac with number 3?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since in the forthcoming testimonies, there will be mention of these UNPA areas or rather places where exchanges occurred, I would like to mark all the places where the exchanges took place. I think that's the best approach. Samac is exactly here, while the River Sava is here so I will mark it with number 1. Sid is approximately here, and the highway runs through this area and this is where Lipovac is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please mark Sid with number 2.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 3 is Lipovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where was Dragalic, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in this zone, there is the place called Nemetin which will also going to be mentioned in relation to the exchange of the 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Nemetin is in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in the UNPA zone east. These areas with lines indicate UNPA zones. Dragalic is on the part of the highway, roughly here. That will be number 5. And in this part here, as I said here there was a Russian battalion and there were Indians in Nemetin. However in Dragalic which is very close, there was a battalion from Nepal. So this is the eastern part of this shaded area and this is Novska which is also going to be mentioned, marked with number 6. There was a Jordanian battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking about these exchange locations, can you tell us where the negotiations with the Muslim part took place most often and where representatives from Samac took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no border line here but this is a kind of demarcation line that ran through this area and this is where Sibosnica was. Satorovici [phoen] was here. And this is Gradacac. And Karanovac near Doboj is also a place that we are going to see on a video film. So towards Tuzla was this demarcation line, and these four locations were on this line that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number 7 for all these four locations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means these were the locations where negotiations were conducted with the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we can see where the negotiations with the Muslim side took place were not under the UN protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another place where negotiations were conducted in which I took part, and that was somewhere here near Glina. This is supposed to be where Petrinja is located, and there was a Belgian battalion there. This is number 8. So all these marked locations and places -- do I have to go back again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the locations where negotiations were conducted at the time in which the commission from Samac took place. There were other, many other places, but we did not have contact with these places except the ones that I just marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number for this exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shaded area here is called Western Slavonia, where you see this place which is called Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The legend says that these were all protected areas so it is clear. Mr. Tadic, we don't have to discuss this document furthermore. Can we have it marked as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D153/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, before we proceed to the exchange of July, tell me where was this exchange to be taken -- to take place in July was agreed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that we did not have any information about these places before that date, and they told us that there was a possibility that in those UNPA zones, safe contacts, either in the form of talks or in the form of exchange, could be secured. We had no experience in that and we couldn't come up with any better proposal so quite simply we accepted this proposal. I very often say "we" and whenever I say "we" I refer to the Serbian part of the negotiating team from Samac. That means either myself or Veljo Maslic or possibly some messages were received by other people than us and we can see that when we speak about the communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to eventually get to Lipovac and make the exchange there, what did you have to do to make the convoy reach Lipovac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that there was this UNPA zone in the map. I didn't show but maybe I should have shown to you where we had to go through in order to reach Lipovac. At the time it was in this UNPA zone which was particularly protected one, and it was inaccessible without the approval of representatives of the United Nations. At the time, they had their offices kind of offices in Belgrade. In addition, we had to go through Brcko, Bijeljina and in Raca we had to cross over to another state, that is Yugoslavia. We had to then go through a part of Yugoslavia which also required permission. So people coming from another state who are not citizens of that particular state, people coming from war-torn zone and of course we needed permission to reach Sid, and also the permission from the United Nations to get to Lipovac. That was really a great problem and I simply went to Belgrade in order to discuss it with the Yugoslav commission, how to accomplish this, because at the time Yugoslavia also had its own exchange commission and I got in touch with some people there who were involved in these matters and they explained to me that we need to have all these permissions that I have just mentioned. They were very forthcoming and they said they would help me in all these matters, that they would get in touch with Yugoslavia and with the United Nations as well, and that they would obtain these permissions for our passage. Of course, that's what they did. I didn't have any contacts with the representatives of Yugoslavia or with representatives of the United Nations. They made a written request for the permission and we did get this permission, I think sometime in late June, for us to be able to cross over to Yugoslavia, pass through these parts of Yugoslavia, and eventually reach the UNPA zone that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the exchange itself, when you were negotiating with the opposite side, and if they have any requests, what did you do if those persons were in detention or were not in detention? What was the procedure? Did you decide it yourself or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained the procedure. I can only repeat it now. The people who were not in detention, and wanted to leave, they applied to the local Red Cross organisation, as for the people who were in detention, permission was given for them by the secretariat or rather the police station or MUP, as we used to call it. So the permission was issued for them by MUP. Of course, those who applied with the Red Cross did not necessarily mean that they would automatically get so to say a visa to leave. Somebody should request them to come from the opposite side in order to put them on the list. So it could have happened that somebody applied but if the -- that person was not sought from the other side, instead of people under -- a man under number 20 as opposed to the man who was first on the list could have been exchanged. This process of seeking went from the opposite side and that is the witness I'm referring to. However, he did not know these men, these people, and he was not able to put anyone in the list to cross over because he didn't know anyone. So that means that somebody ought to suggest to him which particular persons he should seek from our region, and accordingly, he would submit this kind of list to our side and based on that list, and from the one with the applications with the Red Cross already, we took the men who were sought. So that means that somebody could not be -- could not apply for but could have been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even if the people who were not sought but who expressed their desire to go and there were vacant places on the buses, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the number agreed was insufficient, then we would tell him that we have applications from people who wished to cross over, and we would dictate this list to him. Then in turn, he would contact the people on the other side who were supposed to receive these people in Orasje or most often in Samac and Domaljevac on this side because that's where the majority of the residents of Samac were. Then they would say that they knew these people and they didn't know that they didn't arrive or that they expressed their desire in various ways and that is when it could happen that none of those who applied went over, because nobody expressed readiness to receive them and then he would tell us, "I have no facilities provided for this particular person so don't bring there person over."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to a private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this a private session because of the gentleman that we just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me what was the attitude of Mr. Todorovic towards Lukac, towards Bicici and other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a similar attitude towards him as towards the others. He continued to spread rumours that those were very important people, in order maybe to make himself look more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what kind of information did you pass on to the opposite side when these persons were sought for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told them what I knew. I said that there would be problems with getting permission and that as soon as I got one I would put him on so that is what I discussed with them. So regardless of what the opposite side insisted on and sought some people, unless there was permission, this cannot be discussed and vice versa. If we wanted to have some people from the opposite side, if no permission is given, they equally could not have been put on the list. So in each and every case, we need permission from the organs that were conducting investigations or filed reports to the courts. These were organs in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, in order for to you make sense of this information -- sorry, this evidence, you will have to know from whom the permission was being granted. That is in Bosanski Samac. Mr. Tadic has said that on one occasion, Mr. Todorovic was the person granting or not granting permission. But you should know, I submit, whether it was him, that is Mr. Todorovic, on all occasions, who was the man responsible for granting permission for prisoners to be exchanged or whether Mr. Tadic is saying it was Mr. Todorovic or other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness has already said that, at the beginning, but let's clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whom did you apply regarding this? Was it just to him or to somebody else? Who was supposed to give you permissions for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the chief of MUP was in charge of that, and that was Mr. Todorovic, and he could have delegated this authority to some of his associates, to inspectors, police commanders and so on. So he did not have to give permission himself necessarily, but he was in charge of this so to speak. If he withheld his approval, then they were not allowed to do anything without his consent, and in this particular case, I've already said that Mr. Todorovic was absent, and it was quite clear that somebody else was involved in decision-making in that particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So permissions were also requested from some other organs but we will get to that later chronologically?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those first days at the beginning, we mostly applied to SUP for permissions. You will see in the documents that the opposite side sought permissions from the military segment, whereas we did not have that initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we spoke about your entering detention facilities, and you told us that you never went to detention facilities except on one occasion, tell us, please, when and why did you go there? I'm interested in the episode with Mr. Mate Perkovic which you mentioned in your interview.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, when I had a radio contact and was talking to the other side, to the opposite side, I learned that there was a man there who wanted to exchange a few words with me. I didn't know the man. And he told me that his name was Perkovic. I forgot his first name. And that he had a brother detained in Samac, at least that was the information he had, and that is Mate Perkovic, the brother is Mate Perkovic. So he asked me to go and relay the message to his brother to say to him that his family was fine, that there were in a safe place, somewhere in Croatia, I believe, the family was his wife and children, so he just needed to know that they were fine and safe, that he shouldn't worry about them, that he should only worry about himself and that he should try to get on the exchange list. I went to the SUP, and since I didn't know where Mr. Perkovic was kept, I asked the guard on duty to tell me where Perkovic was. He told me that he was there in the SUP building. I told him that I wanted to have a little talk with him and he said that he needed to check with his superiors. He called somebody on the phone and then said to me, "That's fine." And then he went to the SUP building area where two cells were, these two cells were frequently mentioned and shown here, and he took Mato Perkovic to the hallway. I'd never seen the man before. I conveyed the message to him. He thanked me and went back to his cell. That was all regarding my contact with Mato Perkovic. And I would like to emphasise that I didn't know him from before. In 2000, when I was on provisional release, I happened to be in a store selling construction material, and it belongs to a witness called Veselin Blagojevic. Two men came to the store to buy something. I knew one of them very well, and I didn't know the other. And when we greeted each other, he asked me, do you know this man? I said no. He said, this is Mato Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you greet each other then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, we did. In addition to just greeting each other, we also had a little talk and he was very happy about his current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we get to the July exchange, let's cover several other issues, chronologically. In the month of June, did you go to visit Patriarch Pavle in Belgrade and if so what happened there? First, tell me did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to see his holiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session because we will be mentioning a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we will discuss the July exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the following documents together, D12/3, D8/3, D9/3, D71/3, D72/3 and D30/3 ID? The last document is D30/4 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While the documents are being prepared, tell us, please, were there any problems in preparation for that exchange, Lipovac, 4th and 5th July of 1992? How was the final number for the exchange arrived at?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that well because that was practically the first exchange and I remember all of the details well. It was agreed that at around that time, at least the intention was to have that organised as the largest exchange that we ever had with the opposite side. A total of 220 people crossed over from both sides. It was a combination of people, military -- fit for military service, the elderly, women and children, on both sides. That was the category of people exchanged. So it was a combination that we agreed upon in our talks. I assumed that problems would arise in connection with certain persons that were supposed to be exchanged, even one witness said here that one well-intentioned policeman had told him to quickly board the bus and not to peek through the window, which was a sign that somebody was displeased at his leaving. So he was told since he was on the list he should get on the bus quickly and to hide from being seen by other people. Initially, we had problems with [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who created these problems?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a closed or open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to move back again to private session. Just to strike out the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we were late, and I drove my own passenger car, I told them that I will go a little bit forward because my car was faster than the bus in the columns, in order for me to get there in time to advise that we were running late and to make sure that the exchange would take place. I arrived to the place where the Russian battalion was stationed. They were notified about our arrival. I told them that we were running late but they said that they couldn't do anything because they had no contacts from -- with the opposite side, that we had to wait for the police, the UN police to arrive, and since they had communications with them, they called them, the UN police arrived, in fact two policemen came, one of them was a Swede and the other one was an Irishman. We waited there, and I acted as an interpreter as well, and we waited for the buses to arrive for perhaps another hour after I had arrived. So the buses were really -- were pretty much delayed. All the other operations and activities were now taken over by the policemen because they were in contact with the side where Croats were, and they brought some associates of there from Vinkovci and they told us that the other side had been waiting for us since we didn't appear they went back. Then this man told them to go and meet the column, to bring those people back, and if the exchange was impossible to happen on that same evening, that it should happen the following day. So thanks to the UN policemen, it was agreed that the exchange would take place the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few more details relating to this exchange. At the very line of exchange, did persons had to declare their view? You have a list in front of you and can you tell us whether the identical categories of people who cross over on the first occasion --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to say one more sentence about this. That night we had to spend outdoors because this parking lot near the motel was closed at the time, and when I arrived it was already dark. I approached these people, I told them what the situation was, that they should organise themselves somehow, and to have women and children stay in buses and that men should endure this night. We who had cars spent the night on this parking lot until the next morning, just as everybody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on -- because you said that a certain number of men fit for military service, a certain number of elderly men, women and children were agreed. Do these numbers correspond? Are they identical?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is identical, but it happened that in this list, that has kind of marked D12/3, I don't know if it is its -- no, I apologise. I'm looking at another list. That has number 1 in the corner, and there is a list of women --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the document D8/3 ter, beginning with the woman's name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have names of children, specified here, just Milka Stanic and children. It didn't say specifically whether there were two children or more than two children. For example, under number 6, you have Stana Dragojlovic and a child. In this case, it's obvious that there was one child. So if you presume that whenever you have children, there were two children, it turns out that there were more than 40 children involved. And this number was a little bit disputable because apparently there were more children. Amongst Serbs who crossed over to our side. Otherwise, everything is exactly as it had been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with all these six lists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am. And I believe that I had sent these lists to Mrs. Marija Velikonja in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Zaric's counsel, can we ask to have an exhibit number for document D30/4 ID because the remaining documents have already been tendered as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I apologise for that delay. No objections, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D30/4. And ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D71/3 and D72/3 have the same number but I think we have submitted translations of these documents. All right. We shall not waste the Chamber's time now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I make a comment regarding a few names here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We just have to check whether we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't need private session for this and I'm referring to the list, number 3, which begins with the name Kosta, father's name Ljubomir Arsenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honour could we be precisely clear about what exhibit we have in front of the witness, what exhibit we are talking about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is talking now about the document D9/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since yesterday, I mentioned something about this, about these ordinal numbers, 27, 28 and 29. These are exactly the names of my uncles. You can see one was born -- two were born in 1915 and one was born in 1929, and that was particularly the persons who did not apply for the first exchange out of fear because they didn't know what the outcome of the exchange was going to be. So because they were afraid, they remained another two months in detention although they were given priority because much younger people applied than those in this list. However, all these elderly people had bad experience with these events and they were reluctant to apply because of fear and later, they were a little bit upset for having been made to wait another two months because those were old men, as I said, two of them were born in 1915 and one of them was born in 1929.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go -- move to private session just for a couple of moments because we are going to mention a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have a question. Page 31, now it disappeared, but it was lines I think 4, 5 and 6, doesn't make any sense to me. What did the witness intend to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to go back to private session, when the witness told you, "I don't mind having been beaten but I mind having been beaten by Todorovic" that was the comment you made, can you please exchange to the Trial Chamber what did you have in mind? What did this witness actually say?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it was on that page, I said there that the witness, this witness, told me that he didn't particularly mind being in a state he was in and he was in a bad state. We had heard here during testimony that he had been beaten by Mr. Todorovic as well, but since he was an experienced policeman, he knew quite a lot about the police, he told me that he minded the fact that the head of SUP descended so low as to beat him. That was what he minded. He said that the head of SUP would have a lot of ways in getting him in a state he was without affecting himself. So you can conclude what he meant by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like when at the SUP station, the head of SUP would say to his subordinates, "Don't beat him" and then wink at the same time. That's what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, just one more question concerning the July exchange. Did something happen when you got in buses to Samac with people who had been exchanged and those who refused to cross over?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After spending the night in Sid, we completed the exchange, then quite early at that. We returned to Samac, and at the Tekstilac kitchen, a meal was prepared for those who had come from the other side. There were quite a lot of people there waiting. You can imagine what it looks like when some 220 to 230 people come. You can imagine the amount of people waiting to greet them and to see them. So the -- when the meal was already at its end, a shelling of Samac started. Several shells landed in the vicinity of the kitchen, with one of the shells hitting the building itself on the left side. However, there were no casualties, and people simply dispersed, running away from the area. Several people were wounded but there were no fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now take a look at the notebook of the communication centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document PDB 141/3? The problem was that we had two translations, initially I didn't think that it was necessary to translate pages pertaining to the period before the 17th of April, because I didn't think that anything there was relevant for this case, but there are other important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first part I would like to read out is on page 17 of the English version. It's the third paragraph. The date is the 30th of June, 1992. At 900 hours. That's how that sentence begins. And if you have found this, I would like to read it out to Mr. Tadic now. Mr. Tadic, could you please follow what I'm reading and then comment on it? There is a word in the original which has not been translated, so I will read it all out. "On the 30th of June, 1992, at 0900 hours, at conversation with Domaljevac was conducted concerning the exchange. Bozanovic was read out a list of people sought by Orasje. Conversation scheduled for 1100 hours on the same day. Conversation with [redacted]from Odzak was scheduled for 1400 hours. Conversation with [redacted]took place concerning the exchange and a new meeting was scheduled during the day, once [redacted] calls at 2100 hours. Bozanovic conveyed the message to Orasje concerning the exchange. Orasje ready for exchange, providing that the three persons -- providing that the three persons, Tadic wrote down are found. New meeting scheduled for the following day, the 1st of July, 1992, at 0900 hours with Domaljevac." That's at page 14, Mr. Tadic. You will see pagination in the upper corner. Can you tell us, please, as far as I can tell, this coincides with the talks that took place concerning the July exchange. Did you talk to Bozanovic and [redacted]concerning that exchange around that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Marko Bozanovic has been mentioned here in several contexts, so to speak, and one of the contexts was his involvement in exchanges which took place in 1992 and 1993. Since we also had contact with Domaljevac, but that contact was not of the same nature, as the other one from the communication centre, technically it was arranged in a different manner, I didn't really pay attention to that. But at any rate, we were able to establish contact with Marko Bozanovic. I had several conversations with him and the one mentioned here is probably one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to turn to page 16 of the B/C/S version and I suggest that the Trial Chamber turn to page 20, paragraph 4, the 29th of July. That is the date that I will turn to now. On the 29th of July, 1992, talked with [redacted]concerning the exchange. Certain difficulties arose because an exchange commission had been set up on [redacted] side, which is making further work more difficult, as he has less independence in decision-making now. They will meet again tomorrow on the 30th of July, 1992, same time as before. Can we comment on the following, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I failed to find that passage. What date was it, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just listen to what I'm reading, the 29th of July, the 16th page, now listen to my question. On the Bosnian side, Grujicic Milutin is mentioned, a man from Nova Gradiska. I'm interested in this man, Milutin Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to be fair to Mr. Tadic can the usher get the document for him and then you show him which paragraph so that he can follow. I mean if he has to answer questions he must follow the passage you are referring to. The B/C/S version, show him the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic has the original B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, 29th of July, 1992, page 16. Page 16 bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be easier if you had a transcript in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I sat on that chair and I wanted to see what was going on here, I'm trying now to put it on the ELMO so that my fellow accused can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Mr. Usher can you find on that version 29th of July because now we have 29th of August, so just one month before and we shall resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susak was wounded and of course, he was taken prisoner, because of complications to do with his wound, he was transferred for treatment to Belgrade, to the military medical academy. He was taken prisoner in late June. So throughout July, and part of August, he was undergoing treatment in Belgrade, in the institution I have mentioned. After this, when he was much better, he was transferred to the military clinic in Bijeljina, and that's where he was when we discussed him. Although we had approval, however, from high authorities, in this case military authorities, Mr. Todorovic didn't want to organise his transport from Bijeljina to Samac. On several occasions, I asked him to bring him to Samac so that we could organise the exchange. The two exchanges that were to take place before this date in September were not held precisely because this gentleman from Bijeljina had not been brought, and then the other side began to get angry. They said, "Why can't you organise this?" So there was nothing else I could do but go to Bijeljina. I asked that I be given a policeman, a civilian policeman, and that I should go to Bijeljina. I went to Bijeljina with this policeman and of course, we had approval, we had a document, and I found Mr. Susak. I didn't know him. We put him in my car and I drove him to Samac. I was supposed to come to Samac before 1500 hours so that I could talk to (redacted) but I was a little late, and I had just arrived in front of the TO where I was to leave him so that he could spend the night there, when Simo Krunic happened to be there. He's already been mentioned here. He's a policeman. And I said to him, "Simo, here is this man. Look after him. Otherwise, your brother will not be coming tomorrow," because his brother was to be exchanged on the following day. Simo said, "Don't worry, I will sleep with him tonight." Then I went to the communication centre and confirmed that everything was all right now, and that the exchange would take place on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from this document, and from what we know, there was an exchange on the 4th of September. Did it often happen that lists were discussed until the very last moment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document shows this, and very often there were situations due to technical reasons that required discussions until the very last moment. On both sides, there were technical hitches, and someone would always say, "Well we can't do it like this. Let's do it like that."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And my last question in connection with this document, whose duty was it to keep this record? Who entered the information we have just been discussing and that we have put before the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication centre had existed before the war, and it operated according to the legislation then in force. I don't know very much about it but there was an operator there day and night. There was always a duty operator who received and sent certain messages relating to certain situations, and if you look at this, a dispatch arrived, dispatch sent, these are their -- how shall I call them -- documents. These are military things, military matters, that were transmitted through the radio connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these were employees of the Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were employees of the Secretariat for National Defence and had been before the war and continued to be so during the war and they are still there doing something. In this document, you can see that in the beginning, private messages were often received because people learned of this possibility and they used various phone lines to ask about their relatives, because other phones were not functioning so they made inquiries about their relatives, about their friends, and they sent messages through the communication centre for people who were interested in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we mentioned the Maksa from Pelagicevo, what was the full name of this person, his first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Captain First Class, I think, Makso Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you often have contacts with him in connection with the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw each other often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document into evidence and I ask that it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I ask if Your Honours please that it be given an ID number at this stage only. Apparently I'm informed that the -- there have been two translations done of this document, one of which was done here in the ICTY, and that more recent translation does not accord with the translation that the Defence have provided to us, and it's not yet complete, so until that can be done, can it simply be given an ID number and then at a later stage, I suggest that we won't have any objections to it becoming a full exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wish to inform the Chamber both translations are official translations done in the Tribunal. The only difference is that one version is shorter and the other one is complete. In the way they have been formatted there may be some differences but I do agree that the translation should be checked and that we should then have a number given it. I made a mistake, I wanted to help the translation unit, and so I picked out some pages I was interested in so that they would have less work. That's why we have two different versions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one more thing I wish to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Who wants to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic wanted to make a comment but I would first like that we would have the number attached to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we give the number, what I want to ask you, Mr. Lukic is, for your case for the Defence of Mr. Miroslav Tadic, you are relying only on the paragraphs discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I just wanted to demonstrate here a few characteristics aspects but I believe what the whole log is interesting for the Defence, not only because of the line of exchange but especially in the second part, you will see the in document itself that starting from autumn onwards there was no mention of exchanges any more. If you recall, the witness said that when the Bosanski Brod fell, there was no communication going on between the communication centre, but in the radio log, there were daily entries relating to the shelling and this is relevant for the Defence concerning the living conditions in Samac. That is why I believe it should be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be treated as document D 154/3 ID and D154/3 ter ID for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you wanted to comment on something?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to comment a detail referring to the conversation with Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to mention that but the Chamber will have an insight into this part as well. That took place on -- just a moment. Let me find it. Just a second, please. In June, 1992, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to draw the attention to this detail in June, 1992, we had no contacts whatsoever with a part of -- parts of Doboj, Tesanj and Banja Luka. In other words with the western parts, there were no communications and particularly in that period it happened that Dujkovic, a man from our town, was taken prisoner in the area of Tesanj. That is a municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. For the Chamber, page 15, in the translation. This is what Mr. Tadic is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the municipality which is about 40 kilometres to the south from Doboj. We found out that this incident took place, that in fact his father found out because he was our friend and colleague from Samac, and he tried to find a way to establish communication with Tesanj, and that was done through this communication centre. The people from that area, who had been working on these assignments confirmed that Mr. Dujkovic had been captured and we had lengthy conversations with them how to release him, since we had no physical contacts with them. Then they suggested that we from Samac release two men that were kept in prison in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who are they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from Tesanj. I never saw these people before or after. And that is the Muslim parts of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina. After several conversations, they accepted our proposal and released Mr. Dujkovic who then went to the area of Doboj but since we were not able at that time to release the men, we undertook obligation to release them in the next forthcoming exchange, to be carried out in our area, and that happened in July, 1992. These two men left. Therefore, there was really a high level of trust between these two commissions, even though we didn't have a physical commission, we agreed to carry this out, although we had never seen each other, either before that or after that. And in the radio log, on the margin, somebody wrote by hand, and with pencil, those two names, because otherwise, no one would know what had actually taken place. I think it was written there on the margin they left on the 5th of July. I omitted to show those names in the list but maybe it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that you maintained contacts with the opposite side after the July exchange concerning exchanges, but I believe that one incident temporarily had frozen so to say the process of exchange. What happened in July in the area of Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has already been mentioned, that in mid-July, 1992, the Krajina Corps captured the area of Odzak municipality from the River Bosna to the west as far -- to the west towards Zagreb, including the River Sava. So this was a kind of V-shaped area that was under the control of the HVO. So the detainees from Odzak, who were in Odzak, the Serbs detained in Odzak, were transferred to Bosanski Brod. One or two days, they spent in an elementary school in Novi Grad, and after that, they were transferred to Bosanski Brod, a number to the educational centre in Bosanski Brod and the remaining number in the company called Tulek and they spent sometime there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened with the families of those men, their wives and children, of these detainees at the time when the breakthrough of corridor took place, who remained in the territory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When people started to anticipate a war conflict between these two armies, four or five prisoners managed to escape from the elementary school, the ones who had been brought from Odzak, and since they knew the village very well, they found shelter in the nearby woods, and the same was done by the families, the wives and children who happened to be there at the time in Novi Grad. The majority of them found shelter in these areas where they couldn't be found or they went to some cellars and a number of families were taken by the Croatian Army who was withdrawing to Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you like to have some water? I see that you're coughing. Would you like us to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, what we are interested in in this procedure is what became of the population that used to live in this territory before the corridor was broken through?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian population and part of the Muslim population that lived in the town of Odzak, which means that there were no Muslim-populated villages, the entire population withdrew from this area so looking towards Samac, Prud crossed over at the point Skela-Zorica, another went via Skela to Novi Grad, and one via Skela to Kriva. So that when the Krajina units arrived, they virtually didn't find anyone. There were not even any clashes there at the time. I remember very well hearing that from the Krajina fighters, that only two soldiers were wounded and one Croatian soldier was killed but he was not from our region. He was killed in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Croats from the surrounding village of the -- of Odzak municipality leave the area before the arrival of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, from Prud up to Donji Svilaj all the villages were abandoned. That was a rather odd operation that ran in a rather unusual way for an ordinary person, if you look at it how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the names of two ferries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ferries in Zorice, in Novi Grad, and in Donji Svilaj. On the other side of the River Sava, there are places with similar names, there is Slavonski Novi Grad and Slavonski Svilaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where are these places?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- they are in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the witness to be shown the document with the internal mark PDB 30/3. Do you know the date when Odzak fell?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should rather say -- taken by the Army of Republika Srpska. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you see it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time in July, 1992, or somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document again later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have. That was one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you familiar with a name Ivica Matanovic, and who was that man?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know the name of Ivica Matanovic. He was the commander of the 102nd Odzak Brigade. By the way he was a former JNA officer who came to Odzak while those events were in progress but he was originally from our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to have this tendered as an exhibit. With me, I have a copy here. However, the document is in the communication centre in Modrica -- sorry, security centre in Modrica, and I would like this document with a coloured stamp to be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I would like to make some comments on this first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to go into details?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to read this first paragraph, which reads, "All civilian population should be transferred by ferry to Svilaj in an organised manner and tractors with trailers should be transferred from the village via Svilaj, Velika Brusnica [phoen], Bosanski Brod, the bridge Slavonski Brod".

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the population withdrew along these routes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some witnesses before me testified to this, both witnesses for the Prosecution and witnesses for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this route, when you take this ferry to cross over to Svilaj across the River Sava, just make it clear for the Chamber, where does it lead?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections, can we have the number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D155/3 and D155/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, there is no objection to being given an exhibit number but its authenticity is of course by no means accepted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just don't understand, due to the translation that I got is whether the Prosecutor has any objection to the authenticity or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Until there is -- the authenticity of this document is by no means accepted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then can we kindly have the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We've already given it a number, D155/3 ter and D155/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, after the arrival of the Army of Republika Srpska to the territory of Odzak municipality, what do you know what was established then and did you visit this territory of Odzak municipality following the arrival of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After -- in the aftermath of these events, I went to the territory of Odzak. This is nothing unnatural because I originally come from that region, and I both wanted and needed to go there because I wanted to see what the situation was there with the people, with my family, et cetera. It happened sometime on and around the 20th of July. Of course the place was full -- was swarming with army. I went to Odzak and at the checkpoint that had already been established at the entry point to Odzak and there was another one at Jakesnica [phoen], I was told that I had to ask for permission to move around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that when you first came?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On or around the 20th of July, whether it was the 19th or the 20th of July. At the time, the command of the Krajina Brigade was headquartered in, I believe, a hotel. I went there and I met there a major, his name was Mile Peronija [phoen]. He was the head of this brigade, told him what I wanted to see, and he responded that military administration was introduced in the area and that both civilians or members of any other military units had to have permissions to move around. Those permissions were granted on a one-off basis, and after that, one could get a permanent permission. He decided that he can issue a permanent permission to me because I needed to come quite often and he gave me a kind of small ID paper. It resembles a telephone -- pay phone card. And at every checkpoint that had been set up at every two or three kilometres, so one had to pass through four or five of them, there were road obstacles also so one had to show this little card and they would let you go -- pass through. I also heard some more details from him. I asked him whether there were civilians, who did they find, whether anyone was taken prisoner, so that was what I was interested in, and he replied that they had found a small number of women and children and elderly people who were transferred to the reception centre in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 15 or 20, women, children and elderly people at that moment. He also told me that one Muslim was taken prisoner, his name was, I think, Delic, and that he was there in detention in Odzak. Then he added that one Croatian soldier got killed and I immediately wanted to know where that happened and how, and he told me that it happened in the town. When I went to Novi Grad, I had seen that man. His name was Ivan Korade, and I asked him to be buried there so that should the Croats -- should the Croats seek his body, I would be able to hand him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the people who were transferred to Modrica, did you find out their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I finished my visit there, I dropped by in Modrica to this reception centre, and I saw those precisely those people, whom I had already known and some of them I didn't know particularly well, and in conversing with them, I told them that a number of people were exchanged on the 2nd of July, and that there were members of their families in Samac. And I remember that I offered a lift two women by the family name of Aleksic [phoen] and their father-in-law had been exchanged in Samac on the 5th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when and where your fellow citizens from Novi Grad or rather my colleagues are telling me, what was the ethnicity of those people whom you met in Modrica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people in Modrica were Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did the return of Serb families to Novi Grad start, those who had been living in Samac but were originally from Novi Grad and who was this organised by?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were already a lot of people from -- in Samac from Novi Grad. There was the first exchange in May, then the second one on the 5th of July, and that resulted in a large number of people coming to Samac, and then other members of the families arrived there as well, so that there were quite a lot of people, and they wanted to go to their villages as soon as possible. The troops were in their villages at the time. However, the military administration ruled that out, and specified that the return of the civilian population would be possible only when the situation permitted it or rather the conditions permitted it. And that was based on their assessment. So that it wasn't until autumn that the return of these people began. However, they could go for visits, day visits, on an individual basis, and people took advantage of this. They would take a permission, go and visit their village, and then come back within the same day to Samac. It wasn't until later that the conditions permitted for a larger number of people to return to their homes to rebuild the homes, and create everything that was needed for a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The name of Colonel Vujnovic does it mean anything to you? Do you know what he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name sounds familiar, the name of Colonel Vujnovic. I had an opportunity to meet him. He was in the 1st Krajina Corps, in charge of some civilian affairs, I'm not quite sure exactly what he was involved in but it had something to do with civilian affairs and that corps. I remember that on one occasion he came to Samac and met with people from Novi Grad who were gathered there insisting on their return. He explained to them why it was impossible for them to return in large numbers and convinced them that it was impossible, telling them that they should not insist upon it and that as soon as the situation permitted it, he would inform them and they would be able to return to their villages. And to Odzak, naturally, if somebody was from Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These developments concerning Odzak, did that change your attitude in your work with the opposite side concerning exchanges? Did you continue negotiating and organising exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps just in the first few days, there was some kind of a delay, similar to any other crisis, so after the 8th of May, there was a minor delay and then after the 15th of July, there was another delay. However, we knew what we had to do, and we attempted to establish contact if by no other means than using ham operators and we managed to establish contact and continue our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you meet Milutin Grujicic then and what was the relationship between you and the 1st Krajina Corps commission in the work that ensued?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late July, I met Mr. Grujicic. I think that he came to Samac before and met Velimir Maslic but I wasn't there and didn't meet him then. When we started having first talks, that Velimir had arranged with them, then I met Mr. Grujicic in Gradiska which is the town where he lived although he originally was from Okucani in the Republic of Croatia. He lived in Gradiska as a refugee in some apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your cooperation from -- what was your cooperation like from the time you met him and onwards? We will get to Bakovici later but I'm now interested in learning what was your cooperation like. Was that a relationship where one was a superior and the other one was a subordinate or were you equal?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could say that he was our mentor. We relied on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean "we"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the commission from Samac, and all other commissions, there was one in Modrica, in Doboj, in Derventa, and Brod and so on, so all of these commissions relied on him because he had access to the opposite side. He had established contacts with the Nepalese battalion and through the Nepalese battalion we were able to contact the Croatian side directly in the Dragalic area. We were never able to go there on our own. We could never go there on our own initiative to Dragalic and meet with the Croatian side. That was simply not possible. He always had to get a permission in advance, and only upon obtaining the permission from the Nepalese battalion with the list of people were those people who were on the list able to cross over. Naturally, they had to wear civilian clothing and be unarmed, because the Nepalese Battalion supervised the situation very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This Samac commission, what kind of relations did it have with other commissions you have just mentioned? How did they get in touch and what was the reason for them getting in touch?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the commissions in the territory of the former Yugoslavia had an interest to cooperate in the affairs or concerning the affairs we've mentioned here. So as a result of that, we sent our data to other commissions and other commissions in turn sent their data to us. The same was done by the Red Cross chapters. If a Red Cross chapter from some town knew that we would go and negotiate, that they would send us a list, asking us to inquire about those people in our negotiations. So that we, the Samac commission, as well as all other commissions, had tonnes of lists of people from various areas of the war-ridden former Yugoslavia. I remember that I received some lists from Sid, these people asked me to inquire whether some of their fellow citizens were kept elsewhere and so on. Representatives of Orasje got involved in the work of the commission. Later it became known as the Serbian Orasje and people from that area fled to Republika Srpska. Then the next one was Pelagicevo. Those people were together with us, trying to solve their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown Exhibit D91/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for that. I know it by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the documents which circulated around at the time from one commission to the next one. Here at the bottom you can see "commission for seeking and exchanging" and the members of the commission, and then on this right-hand side is the representative of the Red Cross, and these are people from Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are all of these civilian commissions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of these are civilian commissions, commissions for searching for people, and they didn't always know whether all of the people were civilians or in the military. However, they sought them because they were from their area. What is particularly interesting is that information from various sources went to Modrica. For example, they were looking for people that I had on my list, and that perhaps had been exchanged previously, but somebody on the other side was looking for them, unknowing that they had been exchanged and that's why they would send me a list saying this person is sought by many sources. They send these kinds of lists not only to our commission but also to other commissions in Doboj, in Brod, and elsewhere, and you can see it clearly here. It says here, "The people sought from Modrica municipality." You can see that there are Muslims among them, Serbs and Croats. The list of people sought from the Zenica area, a list from Croatia and so on, here on this page, right here, you can see people from Novi Grad who he sought and who had already been on my list, Luba Rakic, Djoko Rakic, and so on. Let me tell you something about this person here, Miroslav Sisljagic I will probably revert back to him later on but Miso Sisljagic is even more interesting. Miso Sisljagic got killed before this date here. He had been killed somewhere in Bosanski Brod. Pero Tadic here had already fled before this date, from a camp or prison in Bosanski Brod, he had already fled and was somewhere in the vicinity of Krajina units at the time. This is Pero's son, who was exchanged later. And so on. You can see people from Gracanica and from other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the documents that circulated among commissions, with the aim of locating these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
