utterances.text: After the June exchange, did something happen in your relations with Mr. Todorovic and the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic and some other individuals, shall I call them, there was something going on with them all the time. Before this and after this. After the July exchange, when Mr. Todorovic returned from the hospital following his treatment, he was very angry that all of this had taken place regardless of him or without his participation, and we couldn't get it undone because it was already done, and he was especially upset that it had been done while he was hospitalised. I don't know where he was hospitalised but he went -- he was in a rehabilitation programme or something like that. At that time, in late July, Captain Jez came to our area, who had found a supporter in Mr. Todorovic. They had similar attitudes. And were able to reach an agreement concerning their further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what unit Captain Jez belonged to? Do you remember what he did?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a security officer but I don't know what unit he was with. He simply moved about our area. He was a member of Krajina Brigades but he was in charge of our area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, in order to follow previous answer of Mr. Tadic's you should be clear about one thing in particular. He says that after the July exchange Mr. Todorovic returned and was very angry that all of this had taken place. I assume that that's a reference to exchanges but if I'm incorrect, then perhaps I could be -- that could be clarified for my -- for the Prosecution's purposes, and in any event it should be, I think, made clear what was he angry about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move into private session for just a few moments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this pertains to the July exchange, and it is clear whom we have in mind. We mentioned a protected witness who was exchanged in July, and therefore, this is what made him angry, the fact that his consent was not asked for, for that July exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he did something to Mr. Cancarevic regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, he harassed Cancarevic as well and I think that he transferred him to Pelagicevo, and after that, Cancarevic was not a commander of police in Samac any more but rather in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a new document, internally marked PDB 31/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume you are very familiar with this document. What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it and this document is one of the consequences of our disagreements. It says here on the basis of unofficial lists submitted by Miroslav Tadic, relating to people planned for exchange. It is the standpoint of this command that a certain number of people cannot be exchanged under present conditions. For someone to prohibit someone from being exchanged, they would have to know these people, because it's impossible for someone to prohibit someone from being exchanged if they didn't know them. So the undersigned, he didn't know these people at all, which means that somebody else had to have told him that these people should not be exchanged, and that was Stevan Todorovic who knew these people because they were detained with Stevan Todorovic, and he acted through this gentleman who signed this document and the -- got this list made because he had quite a lot of influence over this gentleman. I am sure that the undersigned had no idea who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As this list contains quite a number of names mentioned in these proceedings, can you tell us, please, what you did when you received this list? It's addressed to the Crisis Staff. Did the Crisis Staff hold any discussions or reach any decisions in relation to this document, and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was not discussed. It wasn't even registered as having been received by the Crisis Staff. Mr. Mitrovic sent it to me because it's actually addressed to me. So the Crisis Staff did not discuss it, nor was it ever recorded as a document of the Crisis Staff. It wasn't registered. Everybody always referred to the Crisis Staff. So that's what this gentleman thought. He thought that that's what he should put here. But this was actually aimed at me, and against me so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never answered my second question. What did you do when the other side asked for these people on this list and what was your relationship with the military authorities? Would you wait for the end of the question, please? So what was your relationship with the 2nd Posavina Brigade after July, in connection with the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's logical that if I were to send lists there, to be approved, I couldn't put these names, I couldn't put these people down on the lists because that would be counter to the order they had issued. So that we had to wait for this furore to die down a little bit before new exchanges could take place. All the people on this list were ultimately exchanged. Some sooner, some later, but they were all exchanged in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally or the people you worked for ask Captain Jez for his approval after this? Did you ask for the approval for the police apart from what you said about Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After what happened in connection with this document, there was another incident a little later. An official commission was established and although I had not been the President of the commission up to then, because the commission was not formally established and I was not formally appointed its president but because I did the most work on these tasks, I seemed to be the President of the commission that was doing this, and then on the intervention of Todorovic and Jez, who are mentioned here, what happened was that the commission we have already mentioned was established, headed by Velimir Maslic. He found it easier to cooperate with them than I did, because he had a different attitude towards the whole job. His attitude was more professional [as interpreted]. I approached it differently. And of course, for every exchange, you had to get the approval either of the army or of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Mr. Maslic said before this Court about his being present when Mr. Jez was crossing out the names of your relatives? Did Maslic tell you about this at the time? Did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. I learned that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we take a break now? But first of all if there is no objection, I ask that this document be given a number before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D156/3 and D156/3 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall break and continue our proceedings at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a correction of the interpretation, on page 65, line 1, speaking of Mr. Maslic, it says here that he was more professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what word you used exactly, why Maslic was appointed president of the commission for exchanges? What was the word you used?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on why he was appointed, but I used the word, I think, that he was more official in that area, meaning to say that I was more emotionally tied to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You used the word like a clerk or like a bureaucrat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew people from the Odzak -- or rather he didn't know any people from the area of Odzak, or of Samac, because he had not been in Samac long, and he was from Samac. He had arrived some four or five years before these events took place and he didn't know as many people as I did. And that was the difference between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on, I wish to clarify or rather to ask the Office of the Prosecutor as to their standpoint with respect to document D-- the last document, D156/3. I consulted the Prosecution and they said that they do not object to the document being tendered into evidence but that they do contest its authenticity. So I wish to ask the Prosecutor to say why they challenge its authenticity, in view of the fact that the document contains everything that -- according to the rules, so to speak, whenever the authenticity of a document was in question, and during the pre-trial stage, the Prosecution did not object to this document, they should have objected at that stage. If we knew the reasons then we would be able to prove the authenticity of this document. If the Prosecution has no reasons to challenge the authenticity of the document, I submit that the objection should be overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, if Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I had no objection at all to the provision of 156/3. I made no comments on its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So I see. It was misunderstood then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's 156/3. There was a previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 155/3 in which I made the comment that the Prosecution, although not objecting to its going into evidence, is not conceding, that it is authentic, that it is an authentic document, and that's the situation. But as far as 156/3 is concerned, I made no comment relating to its authenticity and I have no objection to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. So that is cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I still have not received the reply. We are discussing document D155/3. I have no explanation as to why the Prosecution is challenging the authenticity of this document. This is not clear to me, because nothing has been said as to why this document is not authentic in comparison to all the other documents that have been tendered so far. The document contains a seal, it has been recognised by the witness, and if the Prosecution has grounds for challenging its authenticity, then it has to give us those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think there is a little bit of confusion here as well, Mr. Lukic, because on page 66, line ten and the following, you actually said D156/3 and wanted comments from the Prosecutor and quite clearly it was on the record as Mr. Di Fazio has just said that they have no objection to 156. So I think that's where there was a little bit of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really think it is not my mistake. I did say document 155. It is probably an error in the transcript. What concerns me is the standpoint taken by the Prosecution on document D155/3, the order of the 11th of July, 1992. This is the document on which I wish to hear the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had certain questions as to the authenticity of this letter. Number 1, the stamp on the B/C/S version, 155/3 ter, is blurred. We can't decipher anything on that stamp. To the right of the stamp is the signature of it. We haven't heard any testimony that this witness was present during the signing of this document, that this witness is familiar with this individual's signature, recognises that to be the signature of Ivica Matanovic. So there is no evidence as to that. With regard to the second option which you have under the theory of authenticity, you can either prove it through direct evidence or you can prove it circumstantially. We haven't received any corroborating evidence as to each one of these things being carried out, that these units were actually seen doing certain things, that any of this did in fact happen, that there is no corroborating information as to any of it. Therefore, based on it being a handwritten document with no evidence as to the signature, as to the stamp, as to any of this, in fact, occurring, it's just as possible this is all a forged document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the Prosecutor's position, allow me to say a few words. A, the stamp mentioned by my learned colleagues can very discernibly be seen on the copy because the copy was made by using a computer from the original. B, the original of the document, I verified through my investigator in the municipal secretariat of the municipality of Doboj in the year 2000, and I have a certified copy here but I don't have an English translation of this certified copy. And C if the Chamber accepts the reasons for this objection as acceptable, then the Defence would propose to hear first of all the investigator for the purpose of our Defence, where he got his document from, and where the document is, and if the Chamber -- and that is that if the Chamber believes that this objection is grounded. However, I think that on no occasion was it ever demanded from witnesses to confirm the signature, if they know the content of the signature -- of the document, it does not necessarily mean that they automatically know the person who had signed the document, for as long as he was speaking this document, and I would like to remind the Chamber here that another two witnesses discussed this document, one for the Prosecution and the witness DW 1/3, that was the witness for the Defence, regarding the facts relating to this document, and I think that the Prosecutor has not offered any substantial reason in order for to us establish the chain and the procedure how this document had been obtained, because we believe that this document is crucial for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If counsel has a certified copy, is it certified from the 102nd Brigade command? What is it -- we can also work on this at the break maybe and not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's what I was about to propose. Why don't Mr. Lukic present the Prosecution with the certification or the latest whatever original that he has and then you can deal with that and also look at the evidence of the witness Mr. Lukic has just mentioned as having discussed some of the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that rather than waste any court time on this, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Also, I think it's important to establish the importance of the contents of this document. They do touch on the evidence of the -- I think demographer on the movement of the population, besides other matters the Defence may be using it for, I think. Maybe that will be sorted out. If not, then we will come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break, I would just like to add that in the document itself the Prosecution stated that the majority of the population had withdrawn from the territory of Odzak municipality, together with the HVO. That was the thesis of the Prosecution. But I think it's best that the parties discuss this document, that we do not waste any more time for the Chamber on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So you can proceed with the rest of the evidence for your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, let us proceed now to the exchanges from August. I'd like you to be shown now the document marked PDB 40/3. And let us concentrate in our further examination on the exchanges that were significant and in which you took part. One such exchange, as the Chamber knows, took place on the 15th of August, and the other one was on the 25th of August. Am I right? Do you remember these two exchanges taking place in August?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember these exchanges, and these documents indicate this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this is the document drawn up by the Croatian commission. On page 3, there is mention of the list of detained women. Do you have any knowledge of this? Do you know of any women being detained on the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of these women from the list I know, especially number 1. Under number 1, we see the name of Milena Dragojlovic, the woman who I mentioned earlier and the one who on the 19th of April, 1992, was captured, together with her husband, and with Milan Rakic, and the other two young men that I mentioned before. Therefore, she was captured and was in Slavonski Brod in detention, wherefrom she was released in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please have a number for this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D157/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like now the witness to be shown Exhibit D130/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the Chamber already knows where Slavonski Brod is located.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody knows it's in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this August exchange was it agreed to accelerate the exchange of elderly people and women? Do you know anything about that, that it was agreed not to hamper this process?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that there were on going talks, we always tried to agree for the flow of these people to be as simple as possible without any major complications and similar things. And in the course of these talks, the dominant topics were, for example, to have the elderly people, the sick people, or the wounded people, to be transferred to the other side as soon as possible in order to be given proper treatment. Similarly, we frequently discussed that it was necessary to work on having separated families and who hadn't yet managed to reunite to work on this issue in order to reunite them as soon as possible on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 2 of this document? You are probably very much familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what is written at the top of the page, pursuant to agreement, at the latest exchange, the opposing sides --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The characteristic thing about this list is that under number 6, there is the woman, Joka Tadic, that is my uncle's wife, and above her is the name of her daughter, Danica Ninkovic. My aunt Joka was born in 1906.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We needn't go further into that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is still alive. And her son was Pero Tadic, the person I just mentioned earlier, and there were many other relatives of hers who were in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now hear from you what I think is rather important about the exchanges and hadn't been mentioned before in this Chamber, and we -- I think we should shed some light on your role in these exchanges. Tell me, what kind of situations did you encounter upon your return from these exchanges? And what were the cases like regarding people who were not exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situations ensuing the exchanges were very difficult ones, especially that was the case in late 1992, when the exchanges did not take place any more in the Samac part of the municipality but rather in the Odzak part of the municipality. It was not our usual practice to say in advance who would be exchanged, so that people would know one or two or five days in advance to read a list, because we were never sure who would be exchanged actually, and we wanted to avoid any mistakes by putting someone on the list and then for that person not to be exchanged. In late 1992, a large number of people from the area of Odzak, pursuant to the permission granted by the military administration, moved to live in this area, especially there were a lot of people from Novi Grad, Dubica, and since a sort of civilian life kind of started to evolve, those exchanges were transferred from Samac to Odzak. In fact we set off from Samac but we returned to the area of Odzak. So instead of going to lunch or to dinner, to the SIT kitchen, the lunch was made in a hotel in Odzak where kitchen was set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please don't go into too many details, just tell me what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where we had -- where those exchanged people had the first contact with their relatives. It goes without saying that people -- these people who managed to cross over were extremely pleased and of course there was no end to the sorrow of those who failed to come as well as to the sorrow of their family members. The people who were dissatisfied saw me as the main culprit for this situation. And all their rage was vented against me in most cases, because the other participants in these processes, they didn't even know. They didn't know Veljo or those men from the Krajina commission, so that I was the main target of their dissatisfaction. It is really hard to describe all these situations. There were even threats made, insults, insults were endless. I remember especially one occasion which was not so vehement, where there were not so many insults. In Dubica, when we arrived at around 3.00 a.m. the bus stopped and two or three men descended, because that was not a large scale exchange and one man approached asking about his son. I told him that I didn't know who his son was, because in this darkness I couldn't recognise him, and I even less knew where his son was, if he wasn't on this exchange, he would be on the next one. The man responded, "Now you're going to exchange everyone because I'm going to bring a rifle" and he went to fetch a rifle. There was a policeman on board the bus, mentioned before, whose name was Pero Krstanovic. Let us not confuse this man with the other man called Perica from Novo Selo. And he instructed the driver to drive on. That was an exchange that took place in January. The driver started the bus so abruptly and he turned around the bend and the man who brought the rifle fired at us, but luckily, he did not hit the bus and we went on. There were numerous situations like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you mentioned January. Was that January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1993. I remember it was winter, it was -- I think on the 7th of January. That was a small-scale exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into details, but what can you tell us about Mihajlo Sisljagic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the names, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before the answer the interpreter says they did not catch all the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say these names. A while ago I said that I was considered to be the one to be blamed for not having all people exchanged in that particular exchange, so in a certain manner, I was to blame. Both by the Serbs, by the Croats and by the Muslims equally. They saw me as the culprit even in the eyes of those who had been exchanged and in the eyes of those who hadn't been exchanged. I was to blame also in the eyes of those who were missing and due to that were not exchanged, and to those who were killed, and were not exchanged, and even in the eyes of those who were first exchanged and that got killed later. A large number of people remained unexchanged -- unexchanged because there was no information, and there is still no information up to this date about their fate. These people are from the Odzak area, Petar Markic went missing in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic do we need these details?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we don't want to go into details but what you've just told us now is quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't wish to go into details but I think it's important to explain what problems Mr. Tadic encountered in his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to give us specific examples, Mr. Tadic, just clarify what you've just said. What led to you being blamed by everybody?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people I started talking about, are those who disappeared in the course of these events. That means that their fate is unknown. The ones I was going to enumerate are registered by the International Red Cross and have their numbers in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, why were you considered the culprit by those who were exchanged and later killed? Why were you blamed by their families?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there were many people who got killed on the opposite side, for whatever reason. I wouldn't like to go into these reasons now. The reasons for them being killed. But they were exchanged after being killed, meaning their bodies were exchanged. Their bodies were brought in and turned over, and I was blamed for not exchanging them earlier, before they got killed. The other ones blamed me that I didn't exchange them while they were alive, nor after they were killed. The third group who were exchanged alive but got killed later, they would say, had he not exchanged them, perhaps they would still be alive today. So these were all different fates of the people who have been mentioned. And somehow, their fates were linked to me -- with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you would have much to tell us regarding this but let us abide by the instructions of the Trial Chamber and focus on other issues important for this trial. I will now focus on the topic that I'm interested in, which is your relationship with the volunteers or the people wearing camouflage uniforms, the so-called Crni who had come from Serbia. There are several brief episodes I would like to hear you describe, but before we turn to that, I would like to hear what was your relationship with Lugar. Yesterday you told us about an episode through which we could see his attitude with respect to you and the people who remained in Crkvina after the massacre. Did you have any other encounters with Lugar and if so, what were they like?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had plenty of encounters, not only with Lugar but also with others, specials if I may call them that. I would just like to add to what Mr. Ljubo Vukovic said when he described the episode when Lugar came to the civilian protection staff. That night, he called me sometime around 2.00 a.m., asking me what I was doing. I told him, "Do you know what people normally do at 2 a.m.? They sleep." And then he started yelling and shouting, you Serbs, what are you like, while I'm creating a state you're sleeping and saying such similar rubbish. And then he said to me, "Make sure you have two or three people ready for me tomorrow who will tell us what they had experienced on the other side," because there was an exchange going on right at about that time. I couldn't mention everything he told me on that occasion. Yesterday, when I went to the staff offices, I happened to pass by two young men who had been exchanged a day or two prior to that event. Those young men were Sveta Goranovic, Svetozar, and another one with the last name Jovanovic. So I told them come with me -- come along with me and you'll have to explain something to somebody. We got there and we ordered coffee and in the meantime, Mr. Lugar arrived. He put a piece of paper in front of them and told them, "Why don't you draw here where the front lines are, where Ustasha positions are and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who said so to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar said that to them and what little they knew they put it on paper. He was quite arrogant and they were a bit scared. And at the end, he asked them, "Did they beat you?" And they said, "Yes." And then he said, "You will come to the detention facility with me, there are Ustashas there and you can beat them all you like." And they said, "Well, how could we go and beat people we don't know, whom we blame for nothing?" And then he jumped and was very angry and his pistol fell out and fired, and what Ljubo said had indeed happened. It hit a hanger. It was enough to have somebody come over for a coffee and talk about something for the pistol to be drawn out. I think that all of that speaks about the attitude he had with respect to people he had a talk with. Naturally, after that, he jumped and started cursing, God knows what, and then he left the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were people from Odzak municipality who did go to detention facilities to beat prisoners? Let me ask you first about these two young men. Do you know whether they went to detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, I know that for a fact. However, he could have come across those who were willing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should make a break now, but before that, the Prosecutor wishes to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, if I may just for the sake of clarity can we get a time frame on this episode with Lugar that the witness describes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, before we rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly but perhaps sometime in August of 1992. We could establish the date exactly if necessary, when Sveta Goranovic was exchanged. We can find his name in the exchange lists. I didn't think this to be particularly important so I didn't research it, but it would be possible to establish when Goranovic was exchanged. At any rate, it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will break now and continue our proceedings at 1500 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you know somebody called Zvezdan? Did you have any encounters with him? Just tell us briefly. We need to cover these episodes as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had hard time going through these episodes. I remember that name, or perhaps it's a nickname. On one occasion, I think it was late June of 1992, around --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, just so that can follow the evidence unfortunately neither my colleague, Mr. Weiner, nor I heard the name of the person and in the transcript it's written Zvezdan -- Zvezdan. If the name could just be repeated so that we could now follow this evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said the person called Zvezdan - Z-V-E-Z-D-A-N - the person has been mentioned during this trial. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know whether that was his first name or his nickname. Around 11.00 p.m., somebody knocked on my door. I remember well there was no electricity, therefore the bell didn't work. I went down, downstairs, and when I asked who it was, they replied, the military police. I opened the door and I saw four unknown to me men. I asked them what they needed and they said, "We will tell you presently." They entered the hallway and then later on we went upstairs. My wife lit the candle and they wanted me to write some kind of a statement, whom I had contacts with, how I established contacts with the other side, did I reveal any military secrets, and similar rubbish. My wife started being angry. She was getting upset, and then Zvezdan said, "I will take the old lady to the other room," for fear of not using a worse word. I asked them, "Do you know who I am?" I wanted to calm the situation down a bit. However, they said, "We don't know but the one who sent us does." In the dark, I wrote the statement. They expressly wanted me to write it in Cyrillic alphabet. After I wrote down some ten lines of the statement, they asked me whether I had arms. I told them I had a pistol. They asked where it was. I said it's hanging on the coat rack. And one of them went there and got the pistol. I told them it was a military pistol. And they said no matter we will give it back to you tomorrow, after you come for additional questioning. They left and I never saw them again. They neither called me nor did I look for them. However, I had occasion to see Zvezdan in Pelagicevo at the military police, when I went to verify whether a young man called Danijel Jovanovic was in prison there. He was sought by the Croats. And he was allegedly captured on our side. I went there intending to see whether he was kept in detention there. When I got there, he looked at me sideways and asked me what I wanted. I said I wanted to inquire about the whereabouts of this soldier. He remembered me. He knew -- he realised that I was the one involved in exchanges, and asked me, "Are you Brko whom I questioned?" I said, "Yes." And he said, "And you're still alive." And I said, as you can see for yourself. And he sent me to a shop to inquire about Jovanovic. He didn't want to send a policeman with me. I went there by myself. And the glass windows of the shop were broken. There were several prisoners in there and I approached the bars on the windows of the shop. I asked whether Danijel Jovanovic was there and a young man approached me and said, "I am that person." And then I told him that he was sought by the Croatian side and I asked him whether he wanted to be exchanged and he said yes. We will probably see this in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please give me direct answers to my questions? When did this incident involving Zvezdan take place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the end of June, 1992, and I said so at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, you mentioned on page 80, line 6, that this person called Zvezdan has been mentioned in the trial. When? I mean, I don't mean every page. I mean that it -- frankly it's not a name that strikes me as being that familiar. Was he a special, paramilitary? I mean who was he, if you could just maybe -- you or through Mr. Tadic, just clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe he was mentioned several times but the freshest instance was when Witness DW 2/3 testified. If you remember, when this specials came, the one who took him to write a statement, he mentioned the name of this person as being one of the specials who had come from Serbia and who made him write the statement. They also wanted to get some money from him, and I don't want to go into details because this all transpired in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's just fine but simply to know, yes, he was one of the specials. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Tadic, Zvezdan was in a group of volunteers or of the people wearing camouflage uniforms who had come from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said at the outset that four men, unknown to me, had come, meaning that all four of them were from Serbia. They were not locals, otherwise I would have known them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in another person from that group, and according to my information, his nickname was Grof, meaning count. Did you have an encounter with him and what transpired there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of those specials, and let me tell you right away, that they never went alone. They usually moved in groups. On one occasion, somebody called Jovo Savic, a deputy commander of the 4th Detachment, informed me that the specials were going around wanting to set on fire a company which was across from my house. It was a carpentry workshop where coffins were made later. He said that they were carrying around a zolja and wanted to fire at that facility. A few minutes went by and some four or five of them came by. They sat at a table. I knew what it was all about so I sat with them trying to calm them down and to prevent the situation from escalating. There were residential buildings all around us and there were many highly inflammable items in that company or workshop, and one of them pointed to that company and said, "Can you see what is written there?" And what it said there was, Comrade Tito, we are -- we give our pledge to you. I never paid attention to that. But then the man said to me, "Have that sign removed within ten minutes." Since I worked at the civilian protection staff, I said that I will get somebody to paint the sign over tomorrow. And then he said to me, "Two minutes have passed." And then I sent two soldiers from the 4th Detachment who happened to be there and told them to try to shoot at the sign from their rifles, to see if it would fall down, to see if the mortar would come off. And they fired at it and somehow managed to get the letters off. In my shop, I still had Tito's picture hanging, the one I described yesterday, and I thought if they should enter that room, they will see Tito's picture and there will be great trouble so I told somebody go into that room take Tito's picture off and the man did it. He hid it behind a chair. However, they never went into that room and they stayed for a few more minutes and then they left, their hand-held grenade launcher remained there and this is how we prevented them from setting that place on fire. There were several other encounters, both involving me and other citizens of Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just thought that if the witness was leaving this episode if we could once again try and get a fix on an approximate time period for this episode.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've already said that it was late June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, no, that concerned the previous incident.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The incident involving Grof, or the count, took place a bit earlier, perhaps early June. I started saying that in addition to the encounters I had with them, there were many other residents of our town who had unpleasant encounters with these men. I remember that our commander, Radovan Antic, also had some problems, as did Makso Simeunovic and Blagoje Simic and Simo Zaric. Perhaps more than one would expect. We've already heard here that whomever they came across and didn't like, they would start slapping or hitting the person, and looking for a pretext to cause trouble. So there were many such encounters and none of them were pleasant. I -- these four men that I just described, a minute ago, Zvezdan and his gang, I saw them frequently in the company of the commander of the 5th Battalion, called Mladen Radovic. In 2000 I asked him whether he had sent these people. I used to see them with him frequently and he told me that he had not sent them. I don't know whether he's to be believed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall now move on to another topic and in order to proceed faster, we have already spoken a lot about the testimonies before the Court so I ask you to answer my questions only briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just before you move on, I wonder, Mr. Tadic, whether you would know, this man, Grof, the count, is he the same person, if you know, that the witness Jelena Kapetanovic mentioned as being somebody who came when she was incarcerated in the stadium and then the cultural centre gymnasium, whatever it was, in Crkvina, if you know? It's just that the name seems to ring a bell in my mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's not the same man, because Jelena was mixed up. It wasn't Grof but another man who came to the detention unit. I think this man's name was Debeli or the fat guy. Grof was so to speak a lower level special purpose man. He didn't have a high post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only ask Mr. Lukic why he's in such a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's because the Defence has to answer the charges so we don't need any more details about the characteristics of some of these people referred to as specials. I think the ones you have narrated, the episodes you have narrated are sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I am putting questions to you which I, as your counsel, consider to be important for your Defence. I believe that you trust me to put proper questions to you, and that we shall stick to what we feel will contribute to challenging the claims of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we shall see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will put a few questions to you about civilian protection and work obligation. We have talked about this before this Court. We have heard testimonies about it, which is why I feel there is no need to go into detail and repeat things. We shall mention only what is essential. This Court has heard quite a lot of testimony about the fact that the premises of the team working on the work obligation were on the ground floor. We heard about the telephone, about the way messages were transmitted, so now I'm asking you: Did you personally or anybody else from the civilian protection staff give any kind of orders to the work obligation service which was housed in the pensioners' club building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only connection between the civilian protection and the work obligation was that we shared the same building and the same telephone. Everything else was separate. No tasks were given to the civilian protection in connection with work obligation unless someone from the civilian protection went to assist by repairing a building or a roof, so if someone from civilian protection helped in something that work obligation was doing, then they would be connected in that way but the civilian protection did not require people to be constantly present as the work that was done was something that happened occasionally, according to need, except for the building of coffins that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you or anyone from the civilian protection able to come in front of the pensioners' club where people gathered for work obligation and then take them away to do something or would you have to apply with a request for this to be approved?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did we do this, nor did we take anyone away. If we needed someone, then one of us would go downstairs to ask Dzevad or Debeli, they are commissioners, whether they had any men available who might be able to help at that moment. If he had people available, he give them to us. If he didn't, then he couldn't. So that was the sort of cooperation we had. And if people were there, and were available, they were happy to go and help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At sessions of the Crisis Staff, the ones what you attended, did you discuss work obligation and did you issue any orders or instructions concerning work obligation to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, we never discussed this at the Crisis Staff, nor did we issue any kind of instructions, because you -- you can tell from what has been said so far how this was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your private vehicle requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My private vehicle, which I used throughout the war, was requisitioned, but I was the only person who used it. This was a kind of perk that we had, because if you had an official car, it was easier to pass through all those checkpoints. You would get a permit, a green-coloured card from the Secretariat for National Defence, containing the details of the vehicle and you would only show that at the checkpoints and then it was easier to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the ministry have used that vehicle for other purposes if they needed it to conduct other business because it was requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In theory but there was no time for them to do that. I don't know when they would do that because I constantly used it. I think I drove over 90.000 kilometres in that car during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, as the commander of the civilian protection staff and the member of the Crisis Staff, were you ever asked anything about the organisation of the procurement of wood for fuel?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These supplies came through the executive board, and it was no secret that that is how fuel or wood was obtained. Citizens who were at risk in any way, such as single mothers, families of soldiers who had been killed, elderly people and so on, who were unable to obtain firewood, they would apply for it and be granted or given firewood by the executive board, and it was they who distributed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself issue orders to anyone to go and collect firewood from the abandoned villages and bring it to warehouses in Samac? You know what the witness Nusret Hadzijusufovic said about this. And I will ask you right away whether you knew any women who lived above Merkur?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never ordered either Nusret or anyone else to do this because there were others who were in charge of that sort of work. So why would I issue orders that were not within my sphere of activity? There was no need for me to do that but I know that firewood was brought in and distributed and that we, as members of the civilian protection staff, had to obtain firewood for our own offices and we did this in the same way as everybody else. We asked the executive board that truck load or two of firewood be brought to us and we used it to heat our premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with the Merkur building, witness Hadzijusufovic testified that he had been ordered to take firewood there to some women who had applied to Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who these women are. There were three such women who lived in a studio flat there. They were refugees from Donja Dubica, there was an elderly woman and her two daughters. One daughter was called Mila and her son was killed in Brod, and that was the basis upon which she asked for firewood and that's why it was supplied to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was her name Goranovic Mara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mila Goranovic, her sister was Mara and the mother's name was Smilja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they ever apply to you with requests for firewood?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. But Granny Smilja always asked about her grandson.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now put a few questions to you about your relations with the Secretariat for National Defence, and the local police, in the period while you held some posts in Samac. At the beginning of your testimony, you said that your son was in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That your son Miroslav was also in the 4th Detachment. Where was he later? And how did you feel about where he was later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said here that my son was in the 4th Detachment. I think this was towards the end of June, when he was sent to a Special Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who sent him there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry for National Defence, the Secretariat for National Defence of Osijek [as interpreted], headed at that time by Bozo Ninkovic. I think it was a big misfortune for parents to have their sons sent to a Special Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... here, unusual here in the transcript on page 90, line 3, it says the Secretariat for National Defence of Osijek and this is definitely not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have that corrected, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretariat for National Defence headed by Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You began to talk about why it was a misfortune for parents to have their son sent to the Special Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this battalion had several names among the people. They called it the intervention battalion and there were other names for it, and you could see from those names that it had a special purpose. Every third soldier of that battalion was killed so one in three was killed, and almost everybody was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to your son?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately he survived, but he was also seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber when your son was seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded on the 19th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally do something to prevent your son being sent to that battalion? Was there anything you were able to do? What was your relationship with the people who sent him there? What did people say about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't do anything, because I felt that I shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any rumours going around Samac and was this considered normal?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people might have talked more if he hadn't gone, but he went and, again, there were stories going around that -- well, but had I asked that he not go, that would not have been seen in a good light.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Was your son later tried, processed? And what was the situation concerning those proceedings? And when was this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in 1993, early 1993. I will be as brief as possible. An acquaintance of mine, a neighbour called Adic, came into our cafe. He was drunk and his 11 year old son was with him and another friend or relative of his. I think his brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you say the man's name was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I only said a neighbour of mine, and an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Slobodan Ilincic. This was at about 1.00 after midnight, 1.00 a.m. and he tried to cause trouble. This man, whenever he got drunk lost control. He didn't get drunk often but on that occasion, his wife was away somewhere and he took the opportunity to get drunk. He tried to hit me, and then my son pushed him and he fell down, and hit a footrest next to the bar and hurt himself. After that, his brother-in-law and his son took him away. He went home first but then he went to the health centre after that, and to make a long story short, on the following day, the police arrived, the civilian police, and they drew up an official record which they were bound to do, and handed this over to the Court and my son was sentenced to four months in prison and 7.000 German marks in damages to that man. I'm saying only that he was not reported -- reported either by the Crisis Staff or the municipal assembly or Blagoje Simic or anyone, but it is well known who can submit a criminal report. The police had to do this ex officio, and that's how my son came to be sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will now move on to a completely different topic. Mr. Tadic, were you a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and you can see this from that document enumerating the members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend sessions of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that it is indisputable before this Court that the municipality resumed its operation in January, 1993. I'm referring to the municipality of Samac. Did you hold any position in the municipal authorities ever since it became operable again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hold any position, before, at the time, or after that. I wasn't a councillor, nor an employee of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up to what time were you the commander of the civilian protection staff and what position did you hold after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian protection staff, as I said at the beginning, covered a whole area of activities, and when the municipality -- municipal authorities became operational, occasionally the duties of the protection -- civilian protection staff were delegated to the municipal organs. We've already seen that the inventory of flats was done by the organs that were established only later. Similarly, when the municipal assembly was established, the protection civilian staff almost had no role any more at the time, because even the building of the coffins that we mentioned in early 1993 also came under the jurisdiction of the executive board and these coffins could not have been gotten free, for free. People had to go to the municipality for kind of certain certificate and with that certificate, they could get these coffins. So if there was any justification for any person to get this coffin for free, then it would be written in the certificate. Otherwise every citizen had to pay for the coffin and then go and collect it there. So, under such circumstances, the Secretariat for National Defence, under which jurisdiction the protection civilian -- civilian protection staff operated, established a new civilian protection staff, which got a so-called normal shape of civilian protection under normal circumstances. People specialised in certain areas, became members of the staff, like people of fire -- for caving in, for fire protection, or for securing the water supply, so about a dozen people were professionally assigned to this civilian protection staff, and the staff moved again back to the communication centre. They were given a female secretary. I think her name was Gordana Tovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what position the defendant held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge, Mrs. Mumba is more interested to hear what was your role and your position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this reorganised staff, I was again for a short time the head, and after that, Perica Krstanovic was appointed to that position and after that, I had nothing to do whatsoever with the civilian protection staff. That staff appointed me a commissioner of a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1993. After that, I didn't have an office or any specific job or any special work obligation with the exception of what I did as a member of the commission for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will talk a little bit more about exchanges later but tell me: Did you take part in any decision-taking process of the War Presidency, and the municipal authorities, after the Crisis Staff started -- ceased to operate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything and what do you know about the incident when people swam across the River Sava in August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there -- there were people swimming across the River Sava in August, 1992, but I didn't believe that as many as 100 people could have swum across the river without anything seeing that so I didn't pay much attention to this story. I didn't believe that that happened, but maybe a few people managed to swim across, but I really couldn't believe that it could have been 100 people, because there were guards there, there were troops there, and I really couldn't believe how that could have happened. But later, in this trial, I heard from many witnesses that this did happen and I accept that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your interview, you also talked extensively and replied to the OTP questions about Zasavica and people being taken away to Zasavica. At the time you didn't mention this incident of swimming across the Sava, but do you believe that these are interlinked incidents? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't have any particulars. I knew that the incident in Zasavica did happen but only later, I realised that that was the reason why those people were taken to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself go to Zasavica in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown the map, 5 -- P9. And I would like to ask the witness to show us where Zasavica is because this is interesting regarding to the first exchange. Can you describe us what was so particular about this village during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to focus here on this area which is interesting. We can't see Samac here. We can only see Zasavica and this is this part of the village. This road leads to Modrica from Samac to Modrica and here there is another road leading to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you just pointed, is that where the bridge is that we saw on the video?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the bridge is. There is no river there. This is just a ravine and this is where the bridge is. And this first house here, once you cross the bridge, that is where -- this is the house belonging to a man named Loncaric and Dr. Ozren Stanimirovic mentioned that and I know very well this man, Loncaric and this house belongs to him and that is where a tavern used to be and we were also colleagues so when you enter Zasavica at this crossroads, there is this artesian well where -- from which the water is supplied and this is where the village is branching so the greater part of the village is on the other side, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark, if you have a pencil, where does -- did this first exchange that we heard of took place? Can you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly, not exactly. When we went to do this exchange, we didn't enter here into the village, but rather we entered more downwards, in order not to disturb the peace of the villagers of Zasavica, not to upset them, so we went down to the road at a lower point and we basically reached the same point by taking a bypass road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark this point with number 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 is place where we took the detour, and number 2 is the place where the exchange was done, and that is where we people crossed over the Bosna and went to the opposite side, to Odzak municipality. At the time, the demarcation lines were somewhere here, running along the River Bosna, and on the other side also along the River Bosna, so when we came close to the river the people stood there and the line was here. We were between these lines and it was very, very dangerous to be in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us: At the time before July, while the demarcation line was on the River Bosna, before Odzak was captured, taken by the Army of Republika Srpska, was that area shelled? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 15th of July, 1992, this is where the demarcation line was, and shells arrived from that side but they never reached the area of Zasavica. The closest they hit the land was somewhere here and this is where one woman got killed. I think that her last name was Sulapovic [phoen] and she is in that list, on that list, and also the postman's house was damaged by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about these villages surrounding Zasavica? Were they shelled in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part -- this part is known as Donja Crkvina and it had also been shelled, and this here is Gornja Crkvina and this part was also shelled, and this intersection also was shelled. This is the road that leads to Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark all these locations with numbers 3, and 4?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Donja Crkvina is number 3, and Gornji Crkvina is number 4, this cluster of houses here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far apart are these -- sorry, how far are these villages are from Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are practically not far away. They are virtually one and the same settlement. You see these two or three houses here, they actually belong to Crkvina, and the houses behind this dotted line belong to Zasavica. So there is virtually no big distance between these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please have the number attached to this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we going to go back to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you further questions but I don't think we need the map any more.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we mentioned this incident of swimming across the Sava and the arrival of these people to Zasavica, I think I need to say a few more sentences about this. In August, when they came in late August, 25th or 26th, of August, at the time there was no demarcation line here. This was a free zone, and people could easily move around to the other side and vice versa. So somewhere here was a pontoon bridge across which it was possible to cross over even in a car to the other side. So at the time, when those people who had been brought from Samac in August, next to this checkpoint that I just mentioned, the whole area was accessible to them. So while this area was under the control of the HVO, people could freely move through village -- down village roads to Crkvina and to Milosevac and because these are the fields that belong to the villagers of Milosevac, Zasavica and Crkvina. So this is to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you just said for the sake of clarity, can you mark with number 5 this checkpoint? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is this house of the man Loncaric who used to run a pub.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what you said that people could freely cross over the pontoon bridge, can you mark that with number 6?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the pontoon bridge and this entire territory was free for movement of civilians from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I wonder if there is a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I haven't misunderstood something. The witness seemed to say that while this area was under the control of the HVO, people could move freely through the village, and at the time his pen was running around the area of the village of Zasavica. Is the witness saying that Zasavica was under HVO control? Because that's the way it reads. It may be that something was lost in the translation. I assume that that may well have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood it but let's have the witness clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to cross over from Zasavica to the territory controlled by the HVO, without any details, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no details whatsoever. All of these matters are very important. Up until the 15th of June, 1992, 15th of July, interpreters correction, the HVO was there, and the positions, the line of the Army of Republika Srpska, were established here, and at that time, it was impossible to cross over to the other side except for that instance when 100 people swam over across the Sava River. And starting in the 15th of July, 1992, there was no HVO on this other side, so this whole area was one and the same, and one could move freely about. Cross over and come back. And this is what happened. The pontoon bridge was here and it was used for people to travel between Samac municipality and Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it would be best if we said for the record that the witness showed that up until the middle of July, there was a demarcation line on the Bosna River and one couldn't cross freely to and fro, the two sides, but after the HVO withdrew from that area, which was on the other side of the Bosna River, people could go freely to the other side, to the other bank of the river.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I also wish to say is that when these people came in late August to Zasavica, this entire area here was open for movement. There were no troops there. There were no demarcation lines so that the only security site was a checkpoint here. Up until the 15th of July, 1992, there was security on this side of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now be given a number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. No objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no objection to the production into evidence of this map. I'm a bit concerned about whether or not we will later be able to marry up the markings on the map to what the witness has said in the transcript but that concern having been expressed, I have no objection to its actual tendering into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D158/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can be verified in cross-examination but I believe that a lot of issues have been now clarified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know the Tomic family from Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I showed the photograph, I've already said that my sister's daughter is married to a Croat from Zasavica, and the house in the picture that we saw can be clearly seen, and that house is right here at this intersection. My friend, Pero Tomic, was on very good terms with me. I went to his house frequently, be it for various parties or some other reason. He was one of the founders of the HDZ in Zasavica village. According to the testimony of the last protected witness, some of the residents of Zasavica and my friend Pero crossed over across the Bosna River and went to the Odzak area. The witness testified that 400 people or thereabouts went from this part of Zasavica and crossed over and that some 70 people remained in the then Zasavica. I had contact with that neighbour of mine, Pero, later on. We used to see each other on the demarcation line after I was indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to these family ties with him, were you on good terms with other residents of Zasavica? We know it to be a village mostly populated by Croats before the war.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of people from that village know me, as I know them. There are a lot of my students living there. In this area right here, we can't see it on the map, but it's visible on that photograph, Marjan Jelavic and Anto Jelavic lived here on this road. There are two houses in the vicinity of the church here. I was on very good terms with them. Anto used to be my roommate when we lived in Samac, and my sister is living in that house as a refugee now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the technical booth now show the excerpt of the videotape regarding Zasavica? We need to see a few details from the beginning of the tape to see whether it has anything to do with what we've just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Does this have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The map?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The videotape, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D142/3, admitted when Dario Radic testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you can comment while the tape is running.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is way too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's rewind back to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the road leading from Samac to Modrica, right here on the right is where you turn to go to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far is this from the centre of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some four to five [Realtime transcript read in error "45"] kilometres. This is the bridge. You can tell that it's fairly narrow, and it's difficult for large trucks to travel across that bridge. We just passed the Loncaric house and then the house we can see in front is the one that belongs to my friend Pero Tomic, this kiosk didn't exist before, it was recently constructed. And here we turn to the left, I showed that on the map just a minute ago and this road now will take to us the church in Zasavica. This is approximately how it looked in 1992, before the 17th. And you can see what it looks like now. Could we continue for just a bit longer? And then we will see a church to the right, but before that, we'll see the house, I think that's what it was, the house belonging to Zecevic, where one of the female witnesses lived. In this part of Zasavica, there were many refugees. We can see the church now. Many refugees from central Bosnia from Sadilovac [phoen]. I believe that some of them are still living there nowadays. And also some people who came as refugees from Odzak municipality. We just missed the church, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe we've seen enough. These refugees that you mentioned, who are still living in Zasavica, what is their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are Serbs from central Bosnia, as I've said, from Sadilovac area, Gostovic and other places, I don't know the names of all of them. And there are also some refugees from Novi Grad and Dubica and other Serb villages in Odzak municipality. I don't know what the situation is like today but I know that my sister is still living there as a refugee, as are some other people. The people who have returned, the Croats from Zasavica, they got their properties back and they either rented them out or they stayed in the village themselves, depending on the arrangements they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I asked you whether you went to Zasavica, you told me no. I was referring to the period after the arrest in August, but I will remind you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to remind me, I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Shall I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you don't have to. On one occasion, when a family named Hodzic from Samac was allowed to cross over the Croatian territory in order to go to France, as their daughter lived in France and was a physician there, their daughter managed, through Marko Bozanovic, to get her mother and sister out, because Marko Bozanovic had some relations with one of these daughters that went to France. So he asked me to bring the Hodzic family to Dragalic because they had a permit issued to them. I was on good terms with Hodzics -- the Hodzic family. Their son worked at school with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you went to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On that occasion, I went to Zasavica to the house of a man where she resided. She got ready, as did her daughter, and based on the papers that I had received from the Red Cross, I took them. I drove them, to Dragalic where their daughter from France was waiting and they departed for France.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that in the summer of 1992, as you stated in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1992. There are documents confirming this. I don't remember the date, didn't stick in my mind, but I think it was summer of 1992 because the weather was fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, just from the point of view of clarity of the transcript, page 102, line 20, you asked Mr. Tadic how far Zasavica is from the centre of Samac. The answer on line 21, I believe I heard Mr. Tadic say four to five kilometres but the transcript says 45. Could you just clarify whether it's four to five or 45?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the witness say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
