utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four to five kilometres. I never measured the distance but some four or perhaps five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I heard you say too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I would like now to turn to several exchanges. The first one I'm interested in is the next one in the chronological order on the 4th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document D3/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which exchange it was? Do you remember any specific details? We mentioned the witness called Zvonko Susak but rather not witness but an individual with that name. We mentioned him. We mentioned the communication centre, and before -- while we are getting the document, do you remember something related to his father that you could tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvonko Susak, as I've already said, was wounded in late June, 1992, when his father was killed. He was unable to locate his father's corpse, and in 2000, when I was at home, he came to see me, asking me to assist him in that endeavour. Since I had some information about the people who were there at the time, they were the people from Novi Grad, I attempted, with a lot of difficulties, to try and locate this. I used another man to establish contacts with Croats. I promised I wouldn't reveal his identity. And then I said I would disclose it to him. So this is how it all came about and he took me to a site, that was perhaps some several square metres large. Later on I showed the site to Zvonko who started digging there and he found his father's body which he later buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this document, now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, could Mr. Tadic specify when in 2000 he spoke to this man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was when I was on provisional release, in Samac. This is when he came to see me. And this is when I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us the people on this list, we've heard a lot of testimony regarding that. Did all of these people have to declare their will to cross over at the exchange site or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them had to declare whether they wanted to cross over or not. That was the typical procedure. We can see that here on this document, where it says that Vukovic, Stipo refused or did not declare his will. Juric, Mato; Cosic, Alija. Juric, Mato is a man from Zasavica. He also declared his will. He remained the -- in Zasavica throughout the entire war and is there nowadays. This other person is from Zasavica as well. I know these people also. They stated that they wished to cross over. Grga Abramovic is on the list of people who were not allowed to leave Samac. This has to do with the document we discussed a little bit ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, let's be more specific. You said that these people had to state their will?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These people had to declare whether they wished to cross over to the Croatian side or not and they said that they did not wish to go to the Croatian side and returned back to Samac and then I've just told you that this man is from Zasavica and is still living there today as are other people listed here who are still living in Samac today. I mentioned Grga Abramovic on purpose because his name was on the other list we just recently discussed and he's living in Holland today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask that the witness be shown document PDB 51/3. Very briefly, are these the persons who on that occasion were handed over by the HVO commission, that is the people who crossed over to your side, and what is their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are Serbs who crossed over to our side. All of them are marked with a plus. None of them went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we be given a number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D159/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Tadic, with respect to this particular document, D159/3 ter, you say that all of them are marked with a plus, none of them went back. With respect, though, to them all being marked with a plus, at least on the Xerox copy I have, a few, such as number 6, Mr. Branko, number 7, Mr. Pero, number 9, Mr. Jovo Ninkovic, et cetera, are marked with minuses and a couple of others as well, not with pluses. And in fact one person, Mr. Savo Savic has neither a plus nor a minus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I will read the names.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the document again? Because I know all the people on that list, down to the last man. And I can tell you about each one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it was just the question you said they are all marked with a plus, that is the thing that is at odds with what's in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I didn't pay enough attention, and now I can say that I didn't pay attention to the pluses, but I know Branko Mikanovic very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I think to make the whole story short, the point is you said that you didn't pay attention to the pluses. Your evidence is that all these people listed were exchanged and were received by your side. That is your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these people crossed over to our side, Savo Savic arrived in the next exchange, not in this one. He arrived in the next exchange, but all of these people crossed over to the Serbian side. So that all the people on this list, I know them personally and they all crossed over to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next exchange list, I will just put a question to you concerning something we heard about before this Tribunal. Do you know whether there were any situations where people who were exchanged or people from the commissions asked you to send them some of their things? And what did you do about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened quite often. Families or people who had left earlier through the commission sent messages, packages, or things that had sentimental value for them. This was no secret. And at the demarcation lines, we usually inspected the things to see what it was that was being taken over, but we allowed this all to pass through, and we would tell people what sort of things they were allowed to send so that we could avoid being brought into an embarrassing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember taking some personal belongings to the family of Juro Krajnovic and what was your relation with that family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often took Juro Krajnovic things prepared for him by his father-in-law, Djordje Ninkovic, and even Djordje himself accompanied me several times to the demarcation line to see Juro. And to talk about their situation, to exchange their views. I have known Juro for a long time, I knew him for 20 years and more although he's considerably younger than me. For a time, he was the director of the Mladost company which was across the road from my house. And I remember that my daughter went to university in Zagreb at the faculty of technology, where she studied the technology of garment making or clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, to shorten things, can you just tell us about your relation with this Krajnovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on friendly terms, on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that his family went to be exchanged with him and were they exchanged in the first exchange, as witness Drljacic, Hajra said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't go to the first exchange. I think it was in September, either on the 16th or the 18th. At any rate in mid-September, that was when they left and that may have been the fourth or fifth exchange. And how this situation arose, I could explain briefly. At the exchange that took place around the 15th or 16th of September, nobody from Samac went to be exchanged. There was only me as a negotiator, because I wanted to establish some details about an exchange. We had already finalised our lists. The lists that we had discussed previously. And obtained approval, and the only thing that was left to do was to establish a date for the exchange. However, from Doboj, they brought some people who were to be exchanged, that they had agreed upon with the Croats, and then there was a hitch, because four people didn't want to cross over to the other side, four Muslims who had arrived from Doboj, they refused to cross over to the other side. And then there was a holdup and the exchange almost failed. There was some members of the international community there, I seem to remember, and this man was very persistent and there was a lot of discussion, and this went on until around midnight. I had no influence on these talks because I was not included, but then I suggested that we should bring four men from the list we had already agreed upon and that rather than waiting for the next date, we should bring the first four men on our list, neither Mijo nor I paid attention to who these people were, we simply said well, the first four names on our list. We could just as well have said the last four names. And then the international police guaranteed that this would take place, and then this exchange took place, the one that we had waited for until midnight. And because we had guarantees for the next exchange, the only problem was to bring these four people on the list, Juro Krajnovic and three other Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that at the time you already had the approval of the police, the SUP in Samac, for these people to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything had already been agreed on except the date of their exchange. The list had already been completed, and all that was left to do was to agree on a convenient date, convenient to both sides, for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because only four men were going to be exchanged, a van was used, but a man's wife, Goja, who is a Serb, came along, and she insisted ongoing too. She wanted to go with her husband, and because there were no obstacles to this, I went to the Red Cross to get a document for her, and this was verified by the Red Cross, so she left with her husband and their two children. The international police was waiting for us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is not important. The witness Hajra Drljacic said before this Court that you took some money from the Krajnovic family for this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never took any money from the Krajnovic family or anyone else but we are now talking about the Krajnovic family. I didn't take any money. This had been agreed on and later on, I remained on very good terms with this Krajnovic and his entire family, and we saw each other very often and his father-in-law's patron saint's day, she said they were one of the first families to leave Samac but in fact, they left only in mid-September, and this is a fabrication just as the fabrication about money.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it time to break for today, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have half a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we continue until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unfortunately we can't get the supporting services beyond this hour, especially the interpretation services. We could only go up to this time. Otherwise, if the services were available, we could certainly have gone up to 7.00. We will adjourn now and continue tomorrow. Mr. Lukic I wanted to know how long are you going to take before you end up your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around two hours. It may be a little more or a little less but I will do my best. I will go through the exchanges and try to finish by the first break tomorrow. I will stick to specific exchanges and avoid going into details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, perhaps to assist the Chamber, I wonder if other Defence counsel might indicate how long they expect to be, if they can give such an indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not the accuseds, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 4.31 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
